title: The Case for Less Eye Contact
author: Tom Geraghty
summary: Geraghty inverts the standard leadership advice that eye contact builds psychological safety, and argues that for many difficult conversations the opposite holds. He sorts workplace conversation into three geometries, facing each other, side by side, and triangulated around a third object, and notes that most guidance treats the first as ideal and the others as degraded. He then assembles the counter-evidence: Argyle and Dean's 1965 equilibrium theory in which gaze, proximity and topic intimacy share one budget, cognitive load research showing that direct gaze competes with speech production and memory, psychophysiological work showing that direct gaze raises arousal, and Goffman's account of face-work as the thing that difficult conversations threaten. The middle of the piece is a tour of settings that already design eye contact out, including walking therapy, Freud's couch, the confessional grille, the barber's chair and the car. Geraghty is careful about the converse finding that reduced eye contact also lowers the cost of cruelty online, and lands on optionality rather than a new rule, since a prescription to avoid eye contact would fail for the same reason the old prescription does.
points: Geraghty maps three physical shapes of conversation and challenges the assumption that facing each other is the superior form.
He revives Argyle and Dean's equilibrium theory to argue that lowering gaze creates headroom for more intimate subject matter.
Cognitive and neurological evidence is marshalled to show that sustained gaze competes with finding words, remembering, and, for autistic participants, threat processing.
The historical survey notes that the police interview room is deliberately built around forced facing, the same arrangement often prescribed for safety.
He flags the disinhibition research showing that absent eye contact also fuels online flaming, so the design goal is reduced facing while keeping people together.
quotes: So here, I thought it'd be interesting to explore a completely different angle on eye contact. What if we could foster greater psychological safety by intentionally reducing eye contact?

Most psychological safety advice assumes the first is the ideal and the other two are somewhat lesser, degraded forms: that a "real" conversation only happens facing each other, maintaining eye contact, with full and intense focus on the person we are in conversation with.

In 1965 Argyle & Dean proposed in Sociometry that intimacy is jointly regulated across gaze, physical proximity, and topic intimacy: i.e. we only have a limited capacity bucket that needs to hold all these things. So by reducing gaze, we can provide more space for topic intimacy.
Reducing eye contact appears to free up cognitive resources to think about how we want to articulate something important.
With difficult conversations, the hard things worth saying are almost always threats to someone's face: ours, theirs, or both.

What all of these share is that the reduction in eye contact is a property of the setting and the context, not a request or accommodation we have to make. Nobody in a walking meeting has to explain why they're not looking at you.
So the arrangement that many LinkedIn posts prescribe for psychological safety is the one interrogators choose for pressure.
The prescription to maintain eye contact fails because it's a prescription; and replacing it with a prescription to avoid eye contact would be flawed in exactly the same way.
